questions.title: How does the 'cumulative effect' doctrine interact with the court's rejection of threats-only claims in *Jimenez*?
questions.question_body: I understand that threats alone usually don't count as persecution (*Karki*). However, Section II.C mentions that courts consider incidents 'collectively' because of their 'cumulative effects.' Why did the Tenth Circuit reject the cumulative argument here? Did the court imply that since none of the individual incidents (threats, a minor assault on an employee, a scare with the child) rose to the level of persecution individually, they couldn't magically add up to something that does? Or is there a different threshold for cumulative harm when no physical injury occurred?

questions.title: What constitutes 'substantial evidence' when an IJ finds a persecutor's motive was financial/professional rather than political?
questions.question_body: In Section II.D, the court affirms that Petitioners failed to show political opinion was a 'central reason' for harm because Don Rafa wanted to protect his drug/revenue interests. The record shows Jimenez was also a Liberal Party supporter. How strict is the 'central reason' test here? If a persecutor has mixed motives (political + business), exactly how small can the political component be before it becomes 'tangential'? Does the fact that they were Liberals initially irrelevant to Don Rafa until he found out about Jimenez's legal work make their political identity legally insignificant in this nexus analysis?

questions.title: Does working for or having family in law enforcement automatically defeat an 'unable/unwilling' government protection claim?
questions.question_body: Section II.E discusses the government's ability to protect applicants. The court notes that Jimenez and his father have connections to the Colombian criminal justice system but didn't report the threats. Is this treated as a waiver of their right to claim government protection? Or is it simply evidence that they knew better than others? The court seems to say that because they didn't try official channels (despite having access), we can't assume futility. Does this create a high bar where having *any* government connection makes it nearly impossible to argue internal displacement is unsafe?

questions.title: Can an applicant rely on hypothetical risks regarding family members remaining abroad to defeat a safe internal relocation finding?
questions.question_body: Regarding Section II.F (Safe Relocation), Petitioners argued they couldn't move internally because their relatives in Colombia might face retaliation due to their own political views. The court dismisses this as 'hypothetical hardships.' For my exam prep: When does an argument about family risk become sufficient evidence versus speculative? If the persecutors explicitly told them to leave only their neighborhood and not their country, why isn't moving elsewhere inherently risky if their entire extended family remains in danger zones?

questions.title: Is there a distinction between 'removal' and 'denial of asylum' when reviewing BIA credibility findings under 8 U.S.C. § 1252?
questions.question_body: The background states Petitioners admitted removability but are appealing only on asylum/withholding grounds. Since the IJ found them credible ('IJ found Petitioners to be credible'), why did they lose on substantive grounds? I am confused about how credibility plays into these specific elements like 'nexus' or 'government protection.' If they are credible witnesses, shouldn't we accept every factual assertion they made? Where does the line fall between accepting testimony as true vs. applying legal standards (like what counts as persecution) to those accepted facts?
